items.title: Ear, Nose, Tongue, and Body: What's Different from the Eye

items.zh: 是中差別者，謂增三、增四。三種耳者，謂肉所纏耳、天耳、審諦耳。四種耳者，謂恒相續耳、不恒相續耳、高聽耳、非高聽耳。
items.en: As for the ear: the same holds throughout as for the eye, save for what is added at the third and fourth kind. The three kinds of ear are: the ear wrapped in flesh, the divine ear, and the attentive ear. The four kinds of ear are: the continuously enduring ear, the not continuously enduring ear, the ear that hears what is lofty, and the ear that does not hear what is lofty.

items.zh: 三種鼻舌者，謂光淨、不光淨、及被損。四種鼻舌者，謂恒相續、不恒相續、有識、無識。
items.en: The three kinds of nose and tongue are: the bright and pure, the not bright and pure, and the impaired. The four kinds of nose and tongue are: the continuously enduring, the not continuously enduring, the one accompanied by consciousness, and the one not accompanied by consciousness.

items.zh: 三種身者，謂滓穢處、非滓穢處、及一切遍諸根所隨逐故。四種身者，謂恒相續、不恒相續、有自然光、無自然光。
items.en: The three kinds of body are: what is a place of impurity, what is not a place of impurity, and what pervasively accompanies and is followed by all the other faculties. The four kinds of body are: the continuously enduring, the not continuously enduring, the one possessing its own natural light, and the one without natural light.

items.title: The Mind, Counted One Through Four Ways

items.zh: 或立一種意。謂由識法義故。或立二種。謂墮施設意、不墮施設意。初謂了別名言者意，後謂嬰兒意。又初謂世間意，後謂出世間意。
items.en: Or it may be established as one kind of mind: that which discerns the meaning of dharmas expressed in language. Or it may be established as two kinds: the mind that falls under conceptual designation, and the mind that does not. The first is the mind that discerns names and words; the second is the infant's mind. Further, the first may also be understood as the worldly mind, and the second as the world-transcending mind.

items.zh: 或立三種。謂心、意、識。
items.en: Or it may be established as three kinds: mind, mental faculty, and consciousness.

items.zh: 或立四種。謂善、不善、有覆無記、無覆無記。
items.en: Or it may be established as four kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-yet-indeterminate, and unobscured indeterminate.

items.title: The Mind, Counted Five Through Seven Ways

items.zh: 或立五種。謂五位差別：一、因位，二、果位，三、樂位，四、苦位，五、不苦不樂位。
items.en: Or it may be established as five kinds, by five distinct phases: first, the causal phase; second, the resultant phase; third, the pleasant phase; fourth, the painful phase; fifth, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant phase.

items.zh: 或立六種。謂六識身。
items.en: Or it may be established as six kinds: the six classes of consciousness.

items.zh: 或立七種。謂依七識住。
items.en: Or it may be established as seven kinds, according to the seven abodes of consciousness.

items.title: The Mind, Counted Eight and Nine Ways

items.zh: 或立八種。謂增語觸相應、有對觸相應、依耽嗜、依出離、有愛味、無愛味、世間、出世間。
items.en: Or it may be established as eight kinds: that associated with the contact of verbal designation, that associated with resistant contact, that grounded in indulgence, that grounded in renunciation, that carrying a savour of craving, that free of any such savour, the worldly, and the world-transcending.

items.zh: 或立九種。謂依九有情居。
items.en: Or it may be established as nine kinds, according to the nine abodes of beings.

items.zh: 或立十種者，無。或立十一種，如前說。或立十二種，即十二心。
items.en: It is not established as ten kinds. It may be established as eleven kinds, as explained before; or as twelve kinds, namely the twelve minds.

items.zh: 謂欲界善心、不善心、有覆無記心、無覆無記心。色界有三心，除不善；無色界亦爾。出世間心有二種。謂學及無學。
items.en: Namely: the desire realm's wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-yet-indeterminate mind, and unobscured indeterminate mind. The form realm has three of these minds, omitting the unwholesome; the formless realm likewise. The world-transcending mind is of two kinds: that of one still in training, and that of one beyond training.

items.title: Form, Counted One Through Five Ways

items.zh: 或立一種色。謂由眼所行義故。或立二種謂內色、外色。
items.en: Or form may be established as one kind: that which the eye operates upon. Or it may be established as two kinds: internal form, and external form.

items.zh: 或立三種。謂顯色、形色、表色。或立四種。謂有依光明色、無依光明色、正不正光明色、積集住色。
items.en: Or it may be established as three kinds: colour, shape, and gesture. Or it may be established as four kinds: light dependent on a source, light not dependent on any source, light that is full or not full, and form that is a mere aggregation.

items.zh: 或立五種。謂由五趣差別故。
items.en: Or it may be established as five kinds, according to differences among the five destinies.

items.title: Form, Counted Six Through Ten Ways

items.zh: 或立六種。謂建立所攝色、覆藏所攝色、境界所攝色、有情數色、非有情數色、有見有對色。
items.en: Or it may be established as six kinds: form comprised in what is founded, form comprised in what shelters, form comprised as an object, form belonging to sentient beings, form not belonging to sentient beings, and form that is both visible and resistant.

items.zh: 或立七種。謂由七種攝受事差別故。或立八種。謂依八世雜說：一、地分雜色，二、山雜色，三、園林池沼等雜色，四、宮室雜色，五、業處雜色，六、彩畫雜色，七、鍛業雜色，八、資具雜色。
items.en: Or it may be established as seven kinds, according to seven distinct matters of attachment. Or it may be established as eight kinds, spoken of together as eight worldly varieties: the varied forms of the earth's surface, of mountains, of gardens, groves, and ponds, of palaces and dwellings, of one's occupation, of painted pictures, of the metalworker's craft, and of ordinary requisites.

items.zh: 或立九種。謂若過去、若未來、若現在、若麁、若細、若劣、若妙、若遠、若近。或立十種。謂十種資具。
items.en: Or it may be established as nine kinds: past, future, present; coarse, fine; inferior, excellent; distant, near. Or it may be established as ten kinds: the ten kinds of requisite.

items.title: Sound, Counted One Through Six Ways

items.zh: 或立一種聲。謂由耳所行義故。或立二種。謂了義聲、不了義聲。或立三種。謂因受大種聲、因不受大種聲、因俱大種聲。
items.en: Or sound may be established as one kind: that which the ear operates upon. Or it may be established as two kinds: sound with a clear meaning, and sound without a clear meaning. Or it may be established as three kinds: sound caused by sentient great elements, sound caused by non-sentient great elements, and sound caused by both together.

items.zh: 或立四種。謂善、不善、有覆無記、無覆無記。或立五種。謂由五趣差別故。
items.en: Or it may be established as four kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-yet-indeterminate, and unobscured indeterminate. Or it may be established as five kinds, according to differences among the five destinies.

items.zh: 或立六種。一、受持讀誦聲，二、請問聲，三、說法聲，四、論議決擇聲，五、展轉言教若犯若出聲，六、喧雜聲。
items.en: Or it may be established as six kinds: first, the sound of reciting and reading aloud; second, the sound of asking a question; third, the sound of teaching the dharma; fourth, the sound of debate and decisive discussion; fifth, the sound of mutual instruction concerning an offence, whether committed or confessed; sixth, the sound of ordinary clamour.

items.title: Sound, Counted Seven Through Ten Ways

items.zh: 或立七種。謂男聲、女聲、下聲、中聲、上聲、鳥獸等聲、風林叢聲。
items.en: Or it may be established as seven kinds: the male voice, the female voice, the low voice, the middling voice, the high voice, the cries of birds and beasts, and the sound of wind through the forest.

items.zh: 或立八種。謂四聖言聲，四非聖言聲。四非聖言者，一、不見言見、見言不見非聖言；二、不聞言聞、聞言不聞非聖言；三、不覺言覺、覺言不覺非聖言；四、不知言知、知言不知非聖言。四聖言者，一、見言見、不見言不見聖言；二、聞言聞、不聞言不聞聖言；三、覺言覺、不覺言不覺聖言；四、知言知、不知言不知聖言。
items.en: Or it may be established as eight kinds: the four kinds of noble speech, and the four kinds of ignoble speech. Ignoble speech: saying one has seen what one has not, or has not seen what one has; saying one has heard what one has not, or has not heard what one has; saying one has sensed what one has not, or has not sensed what one has; saying one knows what one does not, or does not know what one does. Noble speech: saying one has seen what one has seen, and has not seen what one has not; saying one has heard what one has heard, and has not heard what one has not; saying one has sensed what one has sensed, and has not sensed what one has not; saying one knows what one knows, and does not know what one does not.

items.zh: 又有八種。謂四善語業道，四不善語業道。或立九種。謂過去、未來、現在，乃至若遠、若近。
items.en: Further, it may be established as eight kinds: the four wholesome verbal courses of action, and the four unwholesome verbal courses of action. Or it may be established as nine kinds: past, future, present, and so on, down through distant and near.

items.zh: 或立十種。謂五樂所攝聲。此復云何？一、舞俱行聲，二、歌俱行聲，三、絃管俱行聲，四、女俱行聲，五、男俱行聲，六、螺俱行聲，七、腰等鼓俱行聲，八、岡等鼓俱行聲，九、都曇等鼓俱行聲，十、俳叫聲。
items.en: Or it may be established as ten kinds, the sounds comprised in the five kinds of music: first, the sound accompanying dance; second, the sound accompanying song; third, the sound accompanying strings and pipes; fourth, the female voice accompanying performance; fifth, the male voice accompanying performance; sixth, the sound of the conch; seventh, the sound of the waist-drum; eighth, the sound of the cavalry drum; ninth, the sound of the large hourglass-shaped drum; tenth, the actor's cry.

blocks.text: The counting exercise continues: the other sense faculties, then the mind, then the first two sense objects. The most important passages today are the classifications of mind, which bring together the eight consciousnesses in a compact form, and an example from form that our teachers use to explain consciousness-only.

One sentence is missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours) (0292c19–c20): the mind "established as ten kinds: there is none; as eleven kinds, as explained before; as twelve kinds, the twelve minds".

Only the differences from the eye are listed. Among the three kinds of ear is the **attentive ear** (審諦耳). Venerable Miào Jìng: "Listening attentively to the Dharma is called the attentive ear … it is an essential condition for learning the Dharma." Master Cháng Bǎi recalls the Buddha's refrain: "listen closely, listen closely, and reflect well". The body, among other counts, is "what all the faculties follow", since every faculty is located in it.
Two kinds: the mind that falls under conceptual designation (one that discerns names and words) and the mind that does not (an infant's mind); or worldly and world-transcending.

Four kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, **obscured-yet-indeterminate** (有覆無記), and **unobscured indeterminate** (無覆無記). Both teachers assign the third to the seventh consciousness: it is bound with self-view, self-love, self-conceit, and self-delusion, which are too subtle to count as unwholesome, yet they obstruct liberation. The fourth is the eighth consciousness, which is neutral and unobstructed.

Three kinds: **citta, manas, and vijñāna** again (Day 3). Venerable Miào Jìng gives a memorable image: "With manas as support, going outward is called vijñāna. Vijñāna takes in much material and brings it back; flowing back, that is called citta." The six consciousnesses go out to the world; what they gather flows back as seeds into the ālayavijñāna; and the manas stands between as the support.

Seven kinds follow "the seven abodes of consciousness" (七識住). Venerable Miào Jìng: an abode is a place consciousness likes to dwell and does not want to leave; the three unhappy realms are too painful, so they are not counted.

Four in the desire realm (wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, and unobscured indeterminate); three each in the form and formless realms (no unwholesome mind there); and two world-transcending minds (of those in training and those beyond training). Four plus three plus three plus two make twelve. This is a useful map: it shows at once which kinds of mind are possible where.

Form is three kinds: colour, shape, and expressive form (Day 1). It is also five kinds "according to differences among the five destinies". Both teachers explain this with a classic example: humans see water, hungry ghosts see pus and blood, fish see a home, gods see lapis lazuli. Master Cháng Bǎi: "because each destiny's karma differs, each sees the water differently."

This is the "one water, four views" (一水四見) image often used to explain consciousness-only. Notice what it does and does not say. It does not say there is nothing there. It says that what is seen depends on the karma of the seer, so no being sees an object "as it is in itself".

Six kinds by use: reciting, asking, teaching the Dharma, debate, admonition about an offence, and ordinary clamour. Four by moral quality: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, and unobscured indeterminate. Both teachers tell the story of the arhat Pilindavatsa, who called out to a river spirit, "Little servant-girl, stop flowing!" Because he had ended all afflictions, his words were unobscured indeterminate: a leftover habit from five hundred lives in a proud family, with no ill will. Master Cháng Bǎi adds that for a Mahāyāna bodhisattva such words would count as obscured.

Eight kinds: four kinds of noble and four kinds of **ignoble speech**: saying one has seen what one has not, or has not seen what one has, and likewise for heard, sensed, and known. Compare Day 15's four kinds of speech: the same categories, now as a test of honesty.

quiz.q: Among the three kinds of ear is "the attentive ear." How do the two teachers explain it?
options: listening closely and carefully to the Dharma — the Buddha's refrain "listen closely, listen closely, and reflect well"; it is an essential condition for learning the Dharma
an ear that hears very distant sounds
the ear wrapped in flesh
an ear for judging criminals
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Listening attentively to the Dharma is called the attentive ear. In this respect the ear matters — it is an essential condition for learning the Dharma." Master Cháng Bǎi recalls the Buddha's refrain, "listen closely, listen closely, and reflect well on what you hear." B is the divine ear, C the fleshly ear (the supporting organ). Among the four kinds there is also the ear that hears what is lofty — hearing the teaching that turns the ordinary into the noble.

quiz.q: Among the four kinds of mind, to which consciousness do the two teachers assign "obscured-yet-indeterminate" and "unobscured indeterminate"?
options: obscured-yet-indeterminate is the seventh consciousness — bound with self-view, self-love, self-conceit, and self-delusion, neutral yet obstructing liberation; unobscured indeterminate is the eighth
the sixth and the first five
both are the eighth
the eighth and the seventh, respectively
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "'Obscured-yet-indeterminate' … is the four afflictions of the seventh consciousness — also unwholesome, but so subtle that the unwholesome aspect is not evident, so it is called obscured-yet-indeterminate." Unobscured indeterminate is the ripening consciousness. Master Cháng Bǎi (in the Ru-Yi reading note) says the same. D swaps them.

quiz.q: The three kinds of mind are citta, manas, and vijñāna. What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use for their relationship?
options: three brothers
root, trunk, and leaves
past, present, future
with manas as the support, flowing outward is called vijñāna, and flowing back with what it has learned is called citta
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "With manas as support, going outward is called vijñāna. Vijñāna takes in much material and brings it back — flowing back, that is called citta. Flowing out is vijñāna, flowing back is citta, and manas is the support." Master Cháng Bǎi: citta is the ālayavijñāna (accumulator), manas the seventh (pivot), vijñāna the six; the Āgamas use the three loosely, while this system sharpens them.

quiz.q: How are the "twelve minds" made up, according to the treatise?
options: one for each of the twelve links
twelve in the desire realm

four in the desire realm (wholesome, unwholesome, obscured and unobscured indeterminate); three each in the form and formless realms (omitting the unwholesome); two world-transcending (in training and beyond training)
one for each of the twelve sense-fields
quiz.why: "The desire realm's wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, obscured-yet-indeterminate mind, and unobscured indeterminate mind. The form realm has three of these minds, omitting the unwholesome; the formless realm likewise. The world-transcending mind is of two kinds: that of one still in training, and that of one beyond training." 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 12. Master Cháng Bǎi: the higher realms omit the unwholesome because hatred and the like cannot manifest there. Venerable Miào Jìng: the first three fruits are "in training," the fourth "beyond training."

quiz.q: Form is set as five kinds "according to differences among the five destinies." What example do the teachers give?
options: beings of the five destinies have different skin colours
each destiny has its own mountain
each destiny sees the sun at a different size
one water, four sights: humans see water, hungry ghosts pus and blood, fish a home, gods lapis lazuli — different karma, different seeing
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi's lecture: "Take water: humans see water, ghosts see pus and blood, fish see a house, gods see lapis lazuli — because each destiny's karma differs, each sees the water differently." The Ru-Yi reading note gives the same example. It is the classic Yogācāra illustration that the object seen depends on the consciousness seeing it.

quiz.q: "Saying one has seen what one has not, or has not seen what one has" — which kind of sound is this, according to the treatise?
options: the four kinds of noble speech
the four kinds of ignoble speech
the four wholesome verbal courses of action
sound with a clear meaning
quiz.why: "Ignoble speech: saying one has seen what one has not, or has not seen what one has; saying one has heard what one has not, or has not heard what one has; saying one has sensed what one has not, or has not sensed what one has; saying one knows what one does not, or does not know what one does." Noble speech reports each exactly as it was. Venerable Miào Jìng cites an arhat's words, "Whoever knows should answer" — saying "I don't know" when one doesn't is how a noble one speaks. He adds that "sensed" covers nose, tongue, and body, and "known" belongs to the sixth consciousness.
